extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students and general readers of American government and politics
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory textbook material on U.S. taxation, monetary system, national banking, Interstate Commerce Act, and Sherman Antitrust Act; describes legal powers, limits, administrative agencies, and key judicial interpretations. Useful for instructing students about the regulation of finance and commerce in U.S. government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of interstate commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: "The term 'interstate commerce' has been interpreted by a long line of judicial decisions to include the carriage of passengers, the transportation of commodities, and the transmission of ideas, orders, and information by telephone or telegraph from a point in one state to a point in another. In a word, it covers traffic and intercourse in its broadest sense..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text notes that interstate commerce is broad and covers transmission of ideas/info; it explicitly excludes life, fire, and marine insurance and ordinary contractual relations, even though latter may be incident to interstate business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial balancing for state legislation affecting commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: It is very difficult to draw the line between acts affecting commerce wholly within a state and acts affecting commerce between states. The Supreme Court has upheld state legislation primarily designed for legitimate local purposes, although it may impinge at points on interstate traffic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle: state law with predominant local purpose can be sustained despite incidental effects on interstate commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of federal statutes regulating interstate commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutes now in force regulating interstate commerce may be classified into three groups: (1) those controlling railways and common carriers; (2) those designed to prevent trusts and combinations in restraint of trade; and (3) those aimed at miscellaneous objects, such as the pure food law and the law imposing liability on railway corporations for injuries to their employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational rubric for understanding federal commerce regulation and where specific laws fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of the Interstate Commerce Act
rubrics_metrics.description: The Act applies to corporations and persons carrying oil or other commodities (except water and gas) by means of pipe lines, or transporting passengers or property by railway or by rail and water from one state or territory into another state or territory, or from one place in any territory to another place within the same territory, or from any place in the United States to a foreign country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines covered modes and geographic reach; excludes purely intrastate transportation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charges must be just and reasonable
rubrics_metrics.description: All charges for services in connection with transportation of passengers or property must be just and reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fundamental substantive standard enforced under the Act; ICC has authority to determine and prescribe what is just and reasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on free passes/transportation
rubrics_metrics.description: No common carrier can grant free passes or free transportation except to certain specified persons and institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restricts gratuities that could create unfair advantages or favoritism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on carriers transporting commodities in which they have direct property interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Railroad companies are forbidden to transport commodities in which they have a direct property interest, except timber and its products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents self-dealing and conflicts of interest by carriers owning freight commodities (with limited exception).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to construct switches and make connections
rubrics_metrics.description: Common carriers must construct switches and make connections with lateral and branch lines of railways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational duty to ensure adequate network connections and service continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on rebates, drawbacks, and special rates (anti-discrimination)
rubrics_metrics.description: They cannot grant rebates, drawbacks, and special rates, thus discriminating and making lower charges to some persons than to others for similar services; they cannot give any undue or unreasonable preference or advantage to any particular person, company, corporation or locality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core anti-discrimination rule; enforced to preserve fair competition among shippers and localities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on pooling freights and dividing proceeds
rubrics_metrics.description: They are forbidden to make arrangements for pooling freights of different and competing railways, or for dividing among themselves the net proceeds of the earnings of such roads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents collusion among carriers to fix prices or allocate markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and notice requirement for rates
rubrics_metrics.description: They must print and keep open for public inspection schedules showing rates, fares, and charges for transportation, and no change can be made in the rates, fares, and charges so published except after thirty days' notice to the Interstate Commerce Commission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency and procedural notice requirement to prevent secret or sudden rate changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual reporting and uniform accounting
rubrics_metrics.description: They must render full and complete annual reports to the Commission in the manner prescribed by that body; and there is now established one uniform system of railway accounting throughout the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accounting/reporting standard to enable oversight and comparability across carriers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interstate Commerce Commission investigatory powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission is required to investigate the manner in which business is conducted by those carriers to whom the law applies; it may summon witnesses and compel the production of books, papers, and other documents; on request any district attorney must prosecute offenders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ICC has subpoena, evidentiary, and enforcement referral powers for compliance and enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interstate Commerce Commission adjudicatory powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person or corporation complaining of anything done or omitted by any common carrier contrary to the law may apply to the Commission; the Commission may, after full hearing, determine and prescribe just and reasonable maximum rates and charges, as well as just and reasonable regulations and practices; it may award damages to persons injured by a violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ICC can both set rates/regulations and provide remedies for injured parties following hearings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical valuation requirement (1913)
rubrics_metrics.description: Law (approved March 1, 1913) providing for the 'physical valuation' of the property of the railways: the Commission is ordered to 'investigate, ascertain, and report the value of all property owned and used' by such concerns, discover amounts of land and money given to companies by governments, estimate cost of production and reproduction of the property in use, and keep informed as to future extensions and additions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuation standard to inform rate-making and regulatory oversight; requires comprehensive factual accounting of assets and government subsidies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sherman Antitrust Act prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: By this law it was provided that every contract, combination in the form of a trust or otherwise, or conspiracy in restraint of trade or commerce among the several states and territories and with foreign nations was illegal; appropriate penalties were prescribed for violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad statutory prohibition on restraints of interstate and international trade; enforcement requires determining existence of combination/conspiracy and effect on trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial standard for 'undue' restraint (post-1911)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the interpretation of the Supreme Court...in the Standard Oil and Tobacco Trust cases in 1911 the Court laid down the rule that only those combinations which 'unduly' restrained trade violated the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduces a reasonableness threshold: not all restraints are illegal, only those that unduly harm competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation: Sherman Act requires interstate or foreign commerce nexus
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporations or trusts, as such, cannot be regulated unless they are engaged in interstate or foreign commerce in order to come within the terms of the act; e.g., the Sugar Trust case held the Anti-trust law did not control a sugar company that secured a monopoly of manufacture absent direct interstate commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scope-limiting principle: manufacturing monopoly purely internal to states may fall outside Sherman Act unless the conduct has direct interstate commerce effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application when manufacturers divide territory and suppress competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a number of companies engaged in the manufacture of some article form an organization, divide the territory of the United States among themselves for the sale of that article, and suppress competition, the Act applies. The Court held when the direct, immediate, and intended effect of a contract or combination among dealers is the enhancement of prices and suppression of competition, it is a restraint in that commodity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fact-based test emphasizing intent and direct effect on prices/competition rather than mere size or number of states involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application to labor organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Anti-trust Act likewise applies to trade unions whose operations affect interstate commerce; e.g., Loewe v. Lawlor held that when a labor organization by boycott methods affects a manufacturing concern doing a large interstate business, the organization becomes a combination in restraint of trade and is liable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labor activity that has direct effect on interstate commerce can fall within antitrust prohibition; courts have applied the Act to unions in certain contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bureau of Corporations investigatory mandate (1903)
rubrics_metrics.description: Established in 1903 to investigate the organization, conduct, and management of corporations (other than common carriers) engaged in interstate commerce; authorized to subpoena witnesses and documents, administer oaths, require reports, and investigate legal conditions — to collect and make public information for remedial legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative investigatory tool intended to build factual record for enforcement or legislative reform rather than immediate criminal prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional power over money (constitutional and historical limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Constitution, Congress has power to coin money and regulate its value and also to borrow money. Congress is not expressly authorized to issue paper money in any form; historical debates and Supreme Court cases tested constitutionality of legal tender acts during and after the Civil War; later decisions allowed legal tender notes and reissuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains constitutional text, historical practice (legal tender acts, Hepburn v. Griswold, Juilliard v. Greenman), and that Congress may create legal tender notes when deemed necessary, especially under wartime necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: States forbidden to emit bills of credit, coin money, or make anything but U.S. coin legal tender
rubrics_metrics.description: According to the express provision of the Constitution no state can coin money, make anything but gold and silver coin of the United States a tender in the payment of debts, or emit bills of credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limits state monetary action; later judicial interpretation allowed some state-related public corporations to issue paper under narrow readings, but basic prohibition remains a constitutional constraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralization of monetary control via taxation of state bank issues (1866)
rubrics_metrics.description: In 1866 Congress passed an act imposing a tax of ten percent annually on all state bank issues; the tax was upheld by the Supreme Court (Veazie Bank v. Fenno) and thus the states were forced out of the paper money business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative mechanism for federal consolidation of monetary authority—illustrates how fiscal law can effect centralization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of U.S. money (paper and coin) and key instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: The money of the United States falls into two groups: paper and coin. Paper includes United States notes ('greenbacks'), treasury notes, gold certificates, silver certificates, and national bank notes. The whole system was put on a gold basis by act of Congress in 1900.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification useful for understanding legal status and historical evolution of monetary instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: National bank formation and bond-deposit requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Under this system private associations known as national banks may be formed. Each national banking concern is required to deposit with the comptroller of the currency United States bonds equivalent to twenty-five per cent of its capital stock if capitalization is under $150,000, and bonds equivalent to at least $50,000 if capitalization is over $150,000; in turn it may issue national bank notes equal to the par value of the United States bonds so deposited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory and collateral requirement linking note issuance to government bonds to secure currency stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: National bank associations (1908 act) requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: An act was passed in 1908 authorizing the formation of national bank associations (composed of not less than ten banks having an aggregate capital and surplus of at least $5,000,000), and empowering such associations to issue and circulate notes on the basis of certain specified securities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies institutional formation and capitalization thresholds for multi-bank associations intended to increase currency elasticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treasury Secretary authority over depositories and risks
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary of the Treasury is authorized to put portions of the public funds into certain national banks (designated as depositories), on the basis of United States bonds or other satisfactory security; this power allows him to give or withhold the aid of the government in time of stringency, establishing an intimate connection between government and private interests which the text warns is 'full of grave dangers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative discretion with systemic risk and conflict-of-interest concerns; historical examples (Shaw, Cortelyou) illustrate use in crises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treasury Department responsibilities and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: General supervision of taxation and finance is vested in the Secretary of the Treasury, who must scrutinize annual collection and disbursement, master theoretical and practical finance questions, make recommendations to Congress, and secure impartial administration of customs. Work is distributed among assistant secretaries, comptroller of the currency, auditors, treasurer, register, director of the mint, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptive standard of administrative duties and internal division of labor necessary for finance governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on Congressional commerce power (constitutional)
rubrics_metrics.description: This power is subject to the limitation that Congress cannot lay duties on exports from any state, give preference to the ports of one commonwealth over those of another, or compel vessels bound from one state to another to enter, clear, or pay duties in any state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerates express constitutional constraints on federal commerce regulation.
